Sure. Here's something on the small, undervalued craft of noticing.

We live in an age that treats attention like a currency to be harvested. Every app, headline, and glowing rectangle wants a sliver of it. And yet attention is not just money or time; it is closer to a moral act. To pay attention to something is to grant it a little dignity: this street, this backache, this person's hesitation before they answer. The world does not only exist "out there"; it also exists in what we choose to notice.

There is an old pleasure in simply looking. Not looking to optimize, not looking to post, not looking to prove you were there, but looking the way a cat looks at a sunbeam—completely, without announcing a thesis. A pigeon strutting like it owns the pavement. Steam rising from a paper cup in cold air. The oddly moving fact that strangers share bus stops in silence and somehow maintain a tiny temporary society.

Maybe that is why so much writing, good writing, begins with almost nothing: a detail that refuses to be ignored. The chipped mug. The bus driver who says good morning like it's a small public service. The neighbor who waters a single stubborn plant at dawn. Literature often feels grand because of style or theme, but underneath, it is built from attention—from the willingness to stay with the small thing until it opens.

I find it strange and wonderful that a person can read one sentence and suddenly feel less alone inside their own head. Not because the sentence solves anything, but because it recognizes something. Recognition is underrated. Half of comfort is being seen without being explained.

The future will probably bring more speed: faster answers, faster feeds, faster everything. But speed has a way of flattening experience. It makes every moment into a transaction. Attention is the resistance movement. Slow it down. Notice the grain of the table. Notice the change in someone's voice when they talk about what they love. Notice your own mind trying to escape into the next thing, and gently bring it back.

A life is, in some ways, the accumulation of what we repeatedly noticed until it became familiar—and what we refused to notice until it disappeared.

So here's a tiny practice: today, pick one ordinary thing and give it three full seconds of real curiosity. Not judgment. Not use. Curiosity. It won't fix the world. But it might remind you that the world, inconveniently and beautifully, keeps being here whether or not you check it.
